title: Ajahn Funn: Regarding bang-sukun, there is an ancient story. In the suttas, it is said that there was a beautiful woman named Sirimā. The monks…
content:
The Sirimā Story: Contemplating a Corpse Leads to Arahantship

Regarding bang-sukun, there is an ancient story. In the suttas, it is said that there was a beautiful woman named Sirimā. The monks who were still ordinary worldlings (puthujjana), when they saw her beauty, felt lust, desire, and delight to the point that they could not even go for alms. Because of their lust and delight in that form. Later, that woman died, her khandhas ceased. The Buddha used an expedient means: he sent people to invite those monks to contemplate, as explained above.

Bhavobhavā aniccaṃ, dukkhaṃ, anattā – all states of becoming are impermanent. They are just a pool of pus and lymph, like this.

Imaṃ kammaṭṭhānaṃ bhaveti – one must develop meditation by contemplating this. Who would want a form like this? Even if given away for free, who would want it? When those monks went and saw, they felt a sense of spiritual urgency, their minds became calm, and they all attained arahantship. That's how it was.

Therefore, contemplating a corpse has great benefits. That is why monks are invited to perform bang-sukun. But if monks accept the invitation and then go and focus on getting money and gold, that won't work. Huh. It becomes like that. The teachers advise to reflect on kammaṭṭhāna, to contemplate in order to gain great benefits.

title: Ajahn Funn: Right now, our bodily kamma is calm. Our verbal kamma has ceased. Only mental kamma remains. Mental kamma is the act of inclining…
content:
Good Kamma Is a Calm Mind – Bad Kamma Is a Chaotic Mind

Right now, our bodily kamma is calm. Our verbal kamma has ceased. Only mental kamma remains. Mental kamma is the act of inclining and thinking. Whatever kamma we have thought – whether merit or demerit – that kamma is here. Recall this: Kammassakomhi – kamma is my own possession. Kalyāṇaṃ vā pāpakaṃ vā tassa dāyādā bhavissanti – whatever kamma I have done, whether good or bad, I will inherit its result. We must know this. What is good kamma? In short, it is a calm mind, a good mind, with happiness and comfort. That is called good kamma.

And bad kamma (pāpakaṃ)? What is it? It is an unwholesome mind – suffering, chaotic, distressed. That is bad kamma, and we will receive its results in turn.

When you know that something is not good, abandon it. Here we are, old kamma not yet exhausted, and new kamma keeps adding on. Will it ever run out? Stop it. There is no other way to cleanse oneself of demerit and kamma except by sitting in meditation. When our mind is calm, there is no kamma. Where would kamma come from?

title: Ajahn Funn: It is said in the Dhamma-guṇa (qualities of Dhamma): Ehipassiko – one should invite beings to come and see the Dhamma. See what…
content:
Ehipassiko: Come and See Wholesome and Unwholesome Dhamma

It is said in the Dhamma-guṇa (qualities of Dhamma): Ehipassiko – one should invite beings to come and see the Dhamma. See what Dhamma? Wholesome Dhamma and unwholesome Dhamma. Wholesome Dhamma: our mind is good, our mind is wise, our mind has happiness and ease. Every piece of work we do, we want happiness and ease. That is wholesome Dhamma. What is unwholesome Dhamma? It is our mind being not good, suffering, chaotic, troubled. That is unwholesome Dhamma. Let us all know this. The Buddha taught us to invite beings to see this Dhamma. Try calling for suffering from the earth, sky, and weather – there is none. Apart from the mind that suffers, there is none. Happiness also is our mind. Apart from our mind being good, there is no other happiness elsewhere. Evil apart from our mind being evil – elsewhere there is none. Simply put, let us all know through practice. If our mind is not good, then everything becomes not good. If our mind is good, then everything becomes good. Parents, spouses, children ordinarily love each other very much, don't they? If the mind is not good, then everything seems not good, and quarrels arise. If our mind is good, then we do not quarrel.

title: Ajahn Funn: When we contemplate and see in this way, our mind is not deluded, does not have lust or desire for forms (rūpa), because…
content:
Right View: Seeing the Body as Not Self, Not Mine, Not Anyone's

When we contemplate and see in this way, our mind is not deluded, does not have lust or desire for forms (rūpa), because it sees according to reality, according to true understanding. It does not cling or grasp, does not fall into ahaṅkāra (I-making) or mamaṅkāra (my-making) — it is not "me" or "mine," not "him" or "his." Contemplate in terms of paṭibhāga (counterpart, analysis): separate out, break down, scatter away. When our mind contemplates and sees in this way, that is right view (sammādiṭṭhi), it is excellent view, of high value. Like a tree: as long as it remains standing as a trunk and boughs, what value or price does it have? Only when someone takes it, cuts it, splits it, carves it, polishes and smooths it, modifies and assembles it into a useful tool, does it become something of value and price, something everyone wishes and desires to have. We must understand this further. Let us all contemplate this body by way of paṭibhāga — separate it from being a being, from a person, from a self, from an ego, from male, from female, from convention (sammuti) and popular opinion. Separate the head-hairs as just head-hairs; these head-hairs are not a being, not a person, not me, not mine, not him, not his, no one's at all.

title: Ajahn Funn: Those who are prosperous, happy, fortunate, wealthy, beautiful – those are people who have given, who have cultivated virtue and goodness, who have…
content:
Giving, Morality, and Meditation Bring Prosperity and Beauty

Those who are prosperous, happy, fortunate, wealthy, beautiful – those are people who have given, who have cultivated virtue and goodness, who have charity (dāna), morality (sīla), and meditation (bhāvanā). That is, they have built, done, given, and accumulated over many lives and births, not just this life. In this life, some of us don't enter the monastery, don't bow to the Buddha, don't observe the sabbath days, don't keep the holy days. When work is closed, we go out to play, enjoy ourselves, and do not cultivate virtue and goodness. That we come here like this is called coming to cultivate ourselves, to nurture ourselves. The result of this – we are born as people who do not suffer, are not poor. It follows us and leads us through many lives and births. This becomes ingrained as a habit. The result of this is that it makes a person prosperous, happy, and fortunate – not suffering, not poor – because we have done it. It's like a farmer: if he has farmed, he won't starve. If he wants rice to fill his barn and granary, it's full. If he hasn't farmed, even if he wants rice to fill his barn and granary, there is none.

title: Ajahn Funn: Let us all contemplate ourselves and our surroundings. What is there? On mountains and hills there is earth and rock – that is…
content:
The Four Elements: Earth, Water, Wind, Fire – No Self, No Person

Let us all contemplate ourselves and our surroundings. What is there? On mountains and hills there is earth and rock – that is the earth element. There are streams and rivers – that is the water element. There is sky and air – that is the wind element. There is heat and fire – that is the fire element. Look closely: what is the earth element? What is the water element? What is the wind element? What is the fire element? Does it get sick, feel pain, feel hot? Look at fire, do you see? The fire element that cooks food so it digests, that burns the body causing it to deteriorate and decay, or that warms the body – this is called the fire element. We come to dwell relying on these four elements – earth, water, wind, fire – assembled together, and we call it a "self," a "person."

When we separate and analyze the elements, there is nothing at all. Not a single thing. Only elements remain. They reduce to rūpa (form). The physical body consists of these four elements. The mental body (nāma) consists of feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhārā), and consciousness (viññāṇa). What are these things? Contemplate that the khandhas are all impermanent. Feeling is impermanent. Perception is impermanent. Formations are impermanent. Consciousness is impermanent. That's how it is.

title: Ajahn Funn: Contemplate this body. This is the root of the religion. Whoever wants to see Dhamma should contemplate their own conditioned body. When you…
content:
Whoever Sees Dhamma Sees the Buddha – Contemplate Your Own Conditioned Body

Contemplate this body. This is the root of the religion. Whoever wants to see Dhamma should contemplate their own conditioned body. When you see hair, body hair, nails, teeth, skin, and see that these things have no core or substance – that person sees Dhamma. That person studies Dhamma, knows Dhamma, sees Dhamma. Whoever sees Dhamma sees the Buddha. Whoever sees the Buddha will enter parinibbāna, extinguishing suffering in saṃsāra, no longer needing to wander. Those who attained the path and fruit did not study anything else. For example, the five monks of the Pañcavaggiya – the Buddha taught them to contemplate form (rūpa), to contemplate feeling (vedanā), to contemplate perception (saññā), to contemplate formations (saṅkhāra), to contemplate consciousness (viññāṇa). That's all.

When they saw that all these things are impermanent, suffering, and not-self, they attained right there. The mind became calm, it let go. The Buddha asked: Is this conditioned body happiness or suffering? Is it permanent or impermanent? They replied: Impermanent. He asked: That which is impermanent – is it happiness or suffering? They said: Suffering. He asked: That which is suffering – can it be considered a self or belonging to a self? They said: No. Then they let go. Because they let go, they attained.

title: Ajahn Funn: So. Now that you’ve listened to this, try looking at your heart. Try listening to your heart. Is it well or not? You’ll…
content:
Look Inside: Is Your Heart Well or Not? No One Else Can Make It Well for You

So. Now that you’ve listened to this, try looking at your heart. Try listening to your heart. Is it well or not? You’ll recognize it right here. Each of you, now that you’ve listened, look. Is your heart well or not? If you want it to be well, then look at it. I’ve already explained. If it isn’t well, then look at it. If you want it to be well, then make it well. No devas, no Brahmās, can make it well for you.

Our nation is in turmoil, so what can we do? If each of us were to quiet the mind like this, the power of our merit would eliminate danger, eliminate animosity, eliminate poverty, eliminate everything lowly and vile. That’s the way things work: Buddhānubhāvena—through the power of the Buddha, the Dhamma, the Saṅgha. No other power can do it. That’s how our nation can live at peace and at ease. When our hearts are at peace and at ease, the nation is at peace and at ease. After all, the human heart is what creates nations, so the human heart can protect nations (jāti). Jāti—birth—comes from the heart. It doesn’t come from anywhere else.

title: Ajahn Funn: We do not do what is wrong, what is evil kamma. When we do not do evil or kamma, then evil and kamma…
content:
Kamma Is One's Own: Bodily, Verbal, Mental Kamma

We do not do what is wrong, what is evil kamma. When we do not do evil or kamma, then evil and kamma are not in us. Contemplate this. If we dislike evil kamma, we stop doing it. Then evil kamma is not in us. You should carefully consider this point, be certain of it, have confidence in it.

Who is the doer of kamma right now? Contemplate. It is our heart. The Buddha said: kammassakomhi — "I am the owner of my kamma." He said this. Kamma is one's own, not another's. So right now, what kind of kamma are we in? Good kamma or bad kamma? We must contemplate deeply, have confidence. It is not someone else who does it; we ourselves are the doers. Examine it clearly so that we see kamma itself.

Kamma is not up in the sky or air. All the kammas we speak of — this kind of kamma, that kind of kamma, this evil, that evil — evil is not over there or here, in the forest or jungle, in the mountains or woods. They are not evil or kamma. They come from our heart. Therefore the Buddha said: bodily kamma (kāyakamma), verbal kamma (vacīkamma), and mental kamma (manokamma) are ours. Bodily kamma is done through the body, verbal kamma through speech, mental kamma through the mind. This point you should all examine clearly. Do not misunderstand.

title: Ajahn Funn: When we see truly, clearly, and directly, our mind withdraws upādāna, clinging and grasping, or abandons sakkāyadiṭṭhi (personality view). We know that what…
content:
When We See Truly, the Mind Withdraws Clinging and Let's Go of Self-View

When we see truly, clearly, and directly, our mind withdraws upādāna, clinging and grasping, or abandons sakkāyadiṭṭhi (personality view). We know that what we used to grasp as a self, as a being, as a person — as "me" or "him" — is impossible.

When we see like this, the mind becomes peaceful within. It is not entangled in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tactile objects, or mental phenomena. It has no craving for those things. Knowing that they have no core, no essence, no substance, it stops and lets go. This is the crucial point. Then we bring our attention inward to contemplate death. When we see death, we become even more disenchanted. All passion and delight, greed, hatred, and delusion fade away. If we see like this, we find nothing at all as a core or essence, no substance. Then we let go completely. Upādāna — clinging and grasping — ends. And there is no doubt (vicikicchā). There is no sīlabbataparāmāsa — no fondling or clinging to rites and rituals.

So this is why it is said: listen to the Dhamma. Bring it inward, contemplate within yourself, so that you may know and see. The reason the Buddha was able to renounce his royal kingdom was because of this. He attained enlightenment by knowing this — namely, cutting off defilements (kilesa), cutting off craving (taṇhā), lust (rāga), greed, hatred, delusion.
